title: Basil's city of mercy
hookLine: Basil builds a complex of hospitals and hostels outside Caesarea

lines: ROOMS FOR TRAVELERS AND THE SICK.
cards: Outside the walls of Caesarea, in Cappadocia, something is going up that isn't a palace. Rooms for travelers passing through. Rooms for the sick.
Houses for the people who nurse them, workshops, a church. And space for the people the town would rather not see at all: the lepers.
Someone has already complained about it to the governor, and the builder means to answer. The man behind it is Basil, the city's bishop.

teach.h: A NEW CITY OUTSIDE THE WALLS.
teach.b: First, what it was. Not one hospital, but a cluster of buildings with a single purpose: to take in whoever needed taking in. The stranger on the road.
The sick with no family to nurse them. The poor. Gregory, in the speech he gave after Basil's death, tells his listeners to walk out a little way from the city and look at it.
He calls it a new city, a storehouse of godliness, where sickness is seen in the light of faith and compassion is put to the test.
Second, a letter. Someone had spoken against the project to the governor. Basil wrote back.

Who is harmed, he asks, by a church for God, a house for the bishop, and rooms around it for guests and travelers, for those who need care, for the nurses and doctors and workers who serve them? He lets the list speak.
Third, his hands. Gregory says Basil didn't run the place from a distance.
He went to the lepers himself, greeted them, embraced them, treated them as brothers, and urged the well-off to do the same, so that people would stop avoiding them.
Gregory saw Christ honored in the very people others turned away. Fourth, why it lasted.
Mercy here wasn't a mood or a single kind deed. It had walls and a roof and a staff. It would still be there tomorrow.
Catholic hospitals, hostels and shelters carry the same idea: mercy given a building, so it doesn't depend on anyone's good day.

how: Catholic parishes, religious orders and charities run hospitals, shelters and food programs, and Catholics often volunteer in them as one of the corporal works of mercy.

games.q: what does “basil's city of mercy” mean?
o: a new town Basil founded for monks out in the desert
a palace the emperor gave Basil as his bishop's seat
the rooms Basil built for travelers, the sick and lepers

games.q: Basil's city of mercy — tap the pairs.
p: the city outside whose walls it stood

s: Basil's complex stood in the center of Caesarea
it stood outside the walls; Gregory tells people to walk out a little way to see it.
Basil defended the buildings in a letter to the governor
he listed the church, the guest rooms, the rooms for the sick and the people who served them.
Gregory says Basil kept the lepers at a distance
Gregory says Basil embraced them and treated them as brothers.

games.q: you're Basil. someone has spoken against your building project to the governor. what do you do?
o: stop building to keep the peace.
write to the governor and list who the buildings serve.
ignore the complaint and keep going.
games.why: Basil wrote back and asked who could be harmed by rooms for guests, travelers and the sick, and the people who cared for them.

practice: Picture the places near you that take people in: a shelter, a food pantry, a hospital, a parish kitchen, a home for the elderly. Let one come to the front, its door and the people behind it, and stay there a moment.
If you pray, pray for the people who work there and the people they care for.

wordCard.voice: Basil's city of mercy. The rooms for travelers, the sick and the lepers that Basil built outside Caesarea, which Gregory called a new city. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: mercy — the same word family as eleison in the Kyrie at Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: a city of mercy. Kindness, given walls and a roof so it lasts. Until tomorrow.
